newsitem.title: LEBANON: Memories of Israel massacre still fresh in Lebanon.
newsitem.headline: Memories of Israel massacre still fresh in Lebanon.

text.p: The scores of refugees huddled inside a wooden pavilion at a U.N. military base in south Lebanon screamed in terror as a shell exploded nearby.
The next shell crashed into the flimsy structure that served as a chapel for Fijian peacekeeping soldiers, exploding among the refugees and killing dozens of men, women and children.
Scores more died as another pavilion was destroyed as more Israeli shells rained down on the base on April 18, 1996.
In the minds of the Lebanese the Massacre at Qana, as it has come to be known, was one of the worst atrocities in 30 years of Israeli military incursions into their country.
The victims, believed to number about 100, lie in a muddy little cemetery beside the U.N. base that has become a national shrine for the Lebanese.

The massacre was the worst incident in a 17-day bombardment that Israel unleashed on Lebanon on April 11, 1996, killing up to 200 people, causing huge damage and forcing hundreds of thousands of people to flee their homes.

A year later the tragedy still bewilders the Lebanese. They are unable to understand how Israel's vaunted hi-tech army could shell a clearly-marked U.N. peacekeepers' camp crowded with more than 800 refugees.
A U.N. investigation concluded that 17 shells exploded in or around the base and that it was unlikely that the shelling was the result of an Israeli mistake.
Lebanese bitterness is spelled out by a fading poster leaning against the cemetery wall that says: "Qana is the land made holy by Jesus Christ and desecrated by the Zionist satan."

There is a belief in Lebanon that Qana, a town of 35,000 people not far from the Israeli border, is in fact the biblical Canaa in Gallilee where Christ worked his first miracle by changing water into wine at a wedding ceremony.
Ancient rock carvings, apparently of Christ and his apostles, adorn a small valley beside the town, and stone jars that may have held wine and olives lie in the ruins of an ancient building.
Workers are sprucing up the cemetery for the April 18 anniversary, erecting a wall around it and replacing cement tombstones with shiny marble graves.
But the scars are fresh for the people of Qana.

"Why did Israel do this?" asked Mariam Abbas Jaafar, a farmer's wife in a sky-blue jalabiya robe who lost six neighbours in the massacre. "We are civilians, not fighters," she said, looking at the long lines of gravestones.
Only the waist-high cement walls still stand of the pavilion where the first shells exploded. Blackened debris and rain-sodden wreaths lie among the wreckage inside.
At the cemetery, whole families wiped out by the shelling stare out from fading photographs propped against the wall.

In a bare apartment across the road tears stream down the faces of Nawal Ismael Atwi, 46, and her 23-year-old daughter Leila as they speak of the loss of 18 members of the Ismael family and 32 members of the Balhas family into which Leila's sister Gada had married.
Gada died at Qana and her mother and sister say they will wear black until their dying day.
"No. How can you ask?" Nawal replies when asked if she can forgive the Israelis. "They killed our children for nothing. They are terrorists and when I see them I will kill them."

Her curly-haired grandson Hussein, playing beside her, survived the massacre by a miracle. Fijian soldiers found him among the bodies screaming and covered in blood. When he fainted they thought he had died and zipped him up in a body bag.
A few hours later Leila's brother Adnan, who was searching a hospital morgue for his own sons, noticed a body bag moving and found Hussein alive.

Now aged three, he has been to Britain for surgery on his right leg and will have to return for more. "He's not a normal child," says Leila. "We have to hold him and close his eyes to sleep. We can't turn out the light...He destroys his toys and dolls."
Leila is still in shock from losing so many relatives: "I feel lonely. I really feel like I have lost my leg and my arm. They are on my mind all the time," she says.
"Why did it happen, that is the question I ask myself all the time."
